items.bodyEn: Kakegawa was both the twenty-sixth post town and a castle town; Yamauchi Kazutoyo rebuilt its castle in the 1590s. Hiroshige drew the station as a bridge over the Sakagawa with travelers crossing, kites tugging in an autumn wind, and the peak of Mount Akiha, home of a fire-protecting deity, far in the distance.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō (1833–34), No. 27 Kakegawa: Akibayama enbō

items.bodyEn: Pilgrim roads to Mount Akiha, whose deity guards against fire, left the Tōkaidō near Kakegawa, and Akiha worship spread across Edo-period Japan. After a great fire in 1869, Tokyo built a fire-protection shrine on a cleared firebreak; locals nicknamed it after Akiha, the open ground became Akiba-no-hara, and the railway station of 1890 fixed the reading Akihabara.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (日本国語大辞典), entry 秋葉原; Tokyo ward histories

items.bodyEn: 関 is a gate (門) with a bar across it. The ancient character dictionary Shuowen Jiezi defines it as holding a door shut with a crosswise piece of wood. From barring a gate came the checkpoint (関所), the keeper who stands at one (関守), and things bolted together, which is to say a connection (関係).
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entry 關 「以木橫持門戶也」; 新字源

items.bodyEn: This station teaches two patterns for 'while'. Aida ni (間に) simply frames a span: it rained while I slept. Uchi ni (うちに) adds urgency, before this state slips away: eat it while it is still warm. The negative nai uchi ni means 'before': let's go home before it gets dark. Reach for uchi ni when a chance is closing.
items.ja: {温|あたた}かいうちに{食|た}べてね。
items.kana: あたたかいうちにたべてね。
